Pitiful
pĭt´ĭ-fŭl
adj. (full of pity; compassionate — in the KJV a description of the one pitying, not of the one pitied)
English pity + -ful, from Latin pietas through Old French. The KJV sense is active: a pitiful man is one who feels for others. The modern sense, contemptible, is the exact reverse and post-biblical.

Biblical Definition

James applies the word to God Himself: “Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy” (Jas 5:11), having just pointed to “the prophets… for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience” (Jas 5:10). Peter commands it of the church: “be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous” (1Pe 3:8). And Lamentations shows what the siege did to it: “The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children” (Lam 4:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pitiful first as full of pity, tender, compassionate, and secondarily as exciting pity, and then as contemptible — the senses in that order.

expand to see more

PITIFUL, a. Full of pity; tender; compassionate; having a heart to feel sorrow and sympathy for the distressed. James v.

PITIFUL, a. Miserable; moving compassion; as a pitiful condition.

PITIFUL, a. To be pitied for its littleness or meanness; paltry; contemptible; despicable.

Key Scripture

Lam 4:10 — "The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children: they were their meat in the destruction of the daughter of my people."

Jas 5:10 — "Take, my brethren, the prophets, who have spoken in the name of the Lord, for an example of suffering affliction, and of patience."

Jas 5:11 — "Behold, we count them happy which endure. Ye have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy."

1Pe 3:8 — "Finally, be ye all of one mind, having compassion one of another, love as brethren, be pitiful, be courteous:"

Modern Corruption

James points to Job's whole story, not his patience alone, as the proof that the Lord is very pitiful.

expand to see more

James 5:11 makes an argument that is easily missed. He does not say Job was patient and therefore you should be; he says ye have seen the end of the Lord — look at how God finished the story. Job's account contains chapters of unanswered anguish, a wife telling him to curse God and die, friends who accused him wrongly, and a silence from heaven that ran the length of the book. And the end of the Lord was restoration, vindication, and a nearer sight of God than Job had before. James's doctrine is that God's pity is proved by outcomes rather than by the felt warmth of the middle chapters.

The corruption to name is the drift of the word itself, which now means contemptible — and the drift of the idea with it. To pity someone in modern English is faintly to look down on them. The biblical word is the opposite: it describes the Lord, and it is commanded of every Christian toward his brethren in the same sentence as courtesy and brotherly love. Where the church loses the older sense, it tends to substitute either a detached correctness that will not feel, or a sentimentality that feels and does not act. Peter joins the feeling and the manners: be pitiful, be courteous.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek polusplanchnos (G4184), of great compassion, very pitiful; eusplanchnos (G2155), tenderhearted, pitiful; oiktirmon (G3629), of tender mercy.

expand to see more

Greek polusplanchnos (G4184) — very pitiful, of great mercy; James 5:11 only.

Greek eusplanchnos (G2155) — tenderhearted, pitiful; 1 Peter 3:8, Ephesians 4:32.

Greek oiktirmon (G3629) — merciful, of tender mercy; James 5:11, Luke 6:36.

Greek sumpathes (G4835) — having compassion, sympathetic; 1 Peter 3:8 only.

Hebrew rachum (H7349) — compassionate, full of pity; Exodus 34:6, Psalm 103:8.

Usage

"“The Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy” — proved by the end of Job's story."

"“Be pitiful, be courteous” — commanded of the whole church."

"“The hands of the pitiful women” — what famine made of compassion."
